data.title: Alleged Fraudster Drains $800,000 From Iowa Firm in Business Email Scam, Feds Seize $372,583
data.description:
Federal authorities have secured a court judgment forfeiting roughly $375,000 in proceeds from a business email compromise scam that hit an Iowa company in 2022.

The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Iowa issued the order Tuesday after tracing the funds to a Wells Fargo account in the names of Manuel and Ibrahim Hazim, says the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Iowa.

In the scheme, the scammer allegedly posed as vendors of an Iowa company and instructed an employee to send payments to a bank account controlled by the fraudster.

Believing the requests were legitimate invoice payments, the company transferred more than $800,000 to the account in mid-2022. The scammer subsequently moved the money through additional bank accounts in an effort to make the proceeds harder to trace. Authorities ultimately seized $372,583.77 in alleged fraud proceeds from a Wells Fargo account belonging to Manuel and Ibrahim Hazim.

Checks deposited into the account referenced a firm named “Mack Truck” along with “procurement” and payment” in the memo line, yet investigators found no legitimate business activity tied to the deposits.

The Hazims asserted innocent ownership and said the funds were from a currency exchange arrangement but did not provide sworn statements as required.

“Investigation showed that the Hazims did not own or sell a Mack Truck or engage in any other legitimate business transaction with the individual who deposited the funds.”

Says US Attorney Leif Olson,

“Criminals continue to target Americans with email compromise scams. Protect yourself by examining the addresses of incoming emails for differences from previous emails. Follow up in person or by phone to make sure requests are legitimate, especially when someone asks you to change where to send payment. If you or your company are targeted by one of these scams, report it to your bank, to law enforcement, and to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center. We will use every available tool to track down scammers and recover the money they stole.”

data.title: New York Woman Allegedly Impersonates Mother-in-Law for Nearly 17 Years, Defrauds $668,884 in Social Security and Pension Benefits
data.description:
A New York woman has been charged with draining nearly $670,000 in Social Security and pension benefits meant for a deceased relative.

Federal prosecutors say 59-year-old Kimberly Cardella of Rensselaer allegedly wrote herself checks and signed them in her late mother-in-law’s name for nearly 17 years, reports NEWS10.

A grand jury indicted Cardella on bank fraud, theft of government property and aggravated identity theft.

Authorities say more than $530,000 came from Social Security and more than $138,000 from a New York State pension fund, totaling $668,884.

The mother-in-law died in 2009, and because agencies were never told, payments kept landing in her checking account.

Investigators from the Social Security Administration Office of the Inspector General and the New York State Comptroller’s Office uncovered the activity in a joint probe.

Says First Assistant U.S. Attorney John Sarcone,

“The fact that this defendant openly signed her own dead mother-in-law’s name on checks that did not belong to her, in effect adopting her mother-in-law’s identity to obtain public funds intended for those in genuine need is simply shocking.”

Cardella pleaded not guilty at her arraignment and was released on her own recognizance.

If convicted, she faces up to 30 years in prison and a $1 million fine on the bank fraud count alone, plus other penalties and possible restitution of more than $530,000.

data.title: Nearly $2,000 Abruptly Drained From California Woman’s Account via Zelle – But Bank of America Is Refusing To Reimburse
data.description:
A Bank of America small-business customer has lost nearly $2,000 to unauthorized Zelle transfers and says the trillion-dollar bank is refusing to reimburse her.

The longtime customer discovered two payments totaling almost $1,980 to a recipient she did not know, reports NBC Los Angeles.

The California physical therapist, identified as Karleen Cox, says her bookkeeper flagged the June transactions on an account she has held for more than 20 years.

Bank records showed the lender had blocked multiple transfer attempts to the same recipient the day before the successful payments went through.

A phone number tied to that recipient had also been added as an authorized user on the account.

Says Cox,

“It was so obvious and clear that this wasn’t right. Something had happened. Something had been hacked.”

Bank of America repeatedly denied her claim, writing that the transfers used a device consistent with prior valid activity on the account.

On September 22, the bank confirmed to NBC Los Angeles that Cox’s case is closed.

Cox says she took out a loan to cover payroll and is considering small claims court.

“I know to Bank of America, $2,000 may not seem like a lot. But I’m a small business, and $2,000 could be payroll for employees. It’s very impactful for me.”

data.title: Illinois Farmer Defrauds Billion-Dollar Bank Using False Paperwork, Sentenced to Prison and Ordered To Pay $4,966,624 in Restitution
data.description:
An Illinois farmer has been sentenced to 42 months in prison and ordered to repay nearly $5 million after securing about $8.4 million in bank loans with false paperwork.

Travis L. Murphy, 55, of Chandlerville must also serve three years of supervised release, reports WAND.

In 2016 Murphy secured an initial $1,762,000 line of credit from UMB Bank by claiming a grain complex cost about $2.65 million to build when the actual cost was about $986,000, and he also submitted false tax returns.

The false documents led the bank to extend the first loan and later loans that reached about $8.4 million before Murphy tried to wipe out the debts in bankruptcy.

The scheme came to light in U.S. Bankruptcy Court with help from the U.S. Trustee Program and chapter 7 trustee Andrew S. Erickson, and Judge Mary P. Gorman denied the discharge in a 2020 opinion.

A federal grand jury in the Central District of Illinois indicted Murphy for bank fraud in 2023, and he pleaded guilty in 2025.

At sentencing on September 21st, 2026, the court ordered him to pay $4,966,624.01 in restitution to UMB Bank.

News coverage summarizing the government evidence at sentencing said,

“The misrepresentation caused UMB Bank to extend the initial loan and other loans based on that false information and false tax returns Murphy provided to UMB Bank.”

UMB Bank, which is headquartered in Kansas City, Missouri, had approximately $72.35 billion in total assets as of the second quarter, according to the Federal Reserve.

data.title: Bank of America Customer Loses Nearly $6,000 After Scammers Posing As In-House Fraud Investigators Contact Her
data.description:
A Bank of America customer has lost nearly $6,000 after scammers posing as bank fraud investigators and an FBI agent talked her into withdrawing cash and delivering it in a parking lot.

The Florida resident, identified as Susan Trupiano, says the scheme started with a text and a follow-up call from someone claiming to represent Bank of America’s fraud department, reports Gulf Coast News Now.

The callers said they were working with the FBI to probe her local branch and told her they needed her help testing whether a teller was committing fraud.

Says Trupiano,

“Well, little did I know, that was my money they took. They told me they were depositing $6,000, and they wanted me to take $5,500 out because they wanted to make sure that the teller wasn’t committing fraud.”

She was then told to meet a supposed FBI agent in a parking lot, open the back door of a car, and leave the cash on the back seat without speaking to anyone inside.

After she returned home, Trupiano found she was locked out of her banking app and realized her phone had been compromised.

“They hacked my phone, and that’s where all my information was.”

Lee County deputies have been contacted about the case, and no arrests have been reported.

Trupiano says she hopes her story warns others to verify bank and law-enforcement contacts on their own before handing over cash.

data.title: Stablecoin Cross-Border Flows Surge 78% to $220,300,000,000 Amid Crypto Bear Market
data.description:
Cross-border stablecoin transfers are surging nearly 78 percent over the past year even as the broader crypto market experiences a sharp decline.

Transfers of the dollar-pegged tokens across borders climbed from $124.2 billion to $220.3 billion in the 12 months through June 2026.

Monthly volumes more than doubled from $11 billion in January 2025 to $24 billion by June 2026.

The surge occurred even as the total crypto market cap fell 50 percent, a $2.1 trillion contraction that marked the worst bear market since 2022.

The growth came mainly from smaller payments averaging about $3,000, used for supplier payments, sending money home, or moving savings out of volatile local currencies.

New trade corridors opened rapidly, with 4,708 fresh routes carrying $2.64 billion.

The bottom three quartiles of corridors expanded from $0.26 billion to $8.66 billion in value.

Stablecoin balances held steady between $98 billion and $109 billion during the market drawdown, while other crypto assets fell 55.6 percent.

This lifted stablecoins’ share of global on-chain balances to 22.5 percent by June 2026.

The global crypto economy overall contracted just 1.6 percent to $9.4 trillion despite the price slump.

Activity has become consistent, routed through wallets in a steady rhythm rather than in bursts.

“That is the signature of trade and business activity, not speculation,” said Philip Gradwell, vice president of economics at Tether.

He added that the power of USDT lies in serving parts of the economy priced out by traditional finance, at an average cost of one cent per transaction.

“The real power of USDT is in the long tail, the parts of the economy that were priced out or shut out because traditional financial technology was too expensive or too restricted

USDT can serve them because it costs on average one cent per transaction, settles instantly, and needs nothing more than a phone.”

Source: Chainalysis 2026 Global Crypto Adoption Index

data.title: Crypto Exchange Bitget Confirms $351,600,000 Hot Wallet Breach, Abruptly Suspends Withdrawals
data.description:
A leading cryptocurrency exchange is confirming a major security breach involving unauthorized transfers from its hot wallets.

The platform says security systems flagged the abnormal activity at 18:31 UTC on September 24th, 2026, limited to a portion of its hot wallets.

Cold wallets stayed fully secure, and the overwhelming majority of platform assets remained unaffected.

The exchange says it immediately activated emergency protocols and engaged law enforcement along with on-chain security partners.

“Most importantly, user funds remain protected.

The incident falls within the coverage of Bitget’s User Protection Fund, which currently holds more than $464 million.

Customer account balances remain accurate, and deposits and trading continue to operate normally.”

While Bitget says most of the platform’s services continue to operate as usual, it is temporarily halting withdrawals for security purposes.

“As a precaution, withdrawals have been temporarily suspended while our teams complete a comprehensive security review.

We have identified and flagged the relevant transfer addresses and have formally engaged law enforcement agencies and leading on-chain security partners.

We are working around the clock to restore withdrawal services as soon as it is safe to do so.

Bitget will provide further updates through our official channels.”

For now, the crypto exchange says it will not speculate on the attack vector until the investigation is complete.

data.title: Rogue OpenAI AI Agent Breaches Australian Medicare Portal – Aggregate Health Stats Accessed
data.description:
An artificial intelligence agent from a major U.S. tech firm has gained unauthorized access to an Australian government health statistics portal.

The OpenAI model reached the Medicare Statistics Reporting Portal and accessed aggregate health statistics plus internal file names, reports AP News.

The breach took place on June 18th on a public-facing service administered by Services Australia, and no patient records or personal information are believed to have been accessed.

OpenAI says it found the activity in August of 2026 during an internal review of misaligned model behavior, but only notified authorities through a public email inbox on September 10th.

Says OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri,

“We identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation. In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.”

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called the delay unacceptable and held a telephone conversation with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, saying Australia’s extreme concern had been raised directly.

The prime minister told Altman that “it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred, and the nature of the way that notification occurred as well was unacceptable.”

Albanese noted that three other government systems may have been affected, including the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and the Victorian Department of Health.

A forensic investigation with the Australian Signals Directorate is underway, and a taskforce is examining whether other government systems were affected.

data.title: Visa Says Bank-Level Fraud Protection and Deposit Insurance Could Unlock US Stablecoin Adoption
data.description:
Visa is releasing a new report showing how bank-level protections could significantly boost American interest in using stablecoins to send money abroad.

The survey of more than 2,000 US consumers finds that Americans are looking for faster and more affordable ways to send money to family and friends overseas, while still expecting strong security protections.

The company says adoption intent rises from 36% to 56% when stablecoins, or dollar-pegged crypto assets, include fraud protection and deposit insurance, similar to what banks offer.

Nearly two-thirds of respondents say trust depends more on the provider than the technology itself. Meanwhile, willingness to use stablecoins climbs from 36% to 45% when offered through an existing financial institution.

Traditional banks and global payment networks command the highest trust for digital currency services at 61% and 60%, respectively.

Despite the potential rise in US stablecoin adoption, over half of Americans have never heard of dollar-pegged crypto assets, believing prices swing like Bitcoin (BTC).

The report also reveals that 36% of respondents have encountered cross-border payment scams.

The study notes that 44% worry about AI deepfakes impersonating family members and 24% have received AI-generated scam messages that appear real.

About one in five senders cut their own spending to support family abroad.

Says Vira Platonova, Global Head of Visa Direct,

“Remittances are a lifeline—funding education, essentials, and investment back home. Our research shows what matters most to those who rely on that lifeline: trust. The future of the industry will be won by the providers that work hardest to earn that trust.”

The survey notes that stablecoins are not currently covered by deposit insurance such as FDIC, and the protection scenarios are hypothetical.

data.title: Texas Real Estate Investor Masterminds $24,416,911 Fraud Scheme, Sentenced to 188 Months Behind Bars
data.description:
A federal judge has sentenced a Dallas real estate investor to more than 15 years in prison and ordered repayment of over $24 million after he admitted to running a long-running fraud that victimized more than 80 people.

Charles Carrier, 67, received the 188-month term from US District Judge Brantley Starr and must pay $24,416,911.16 in restitution, says the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas.

Carrier pleaded guilty last year to wire fraud for soliciting investor money he claimed would fund the purchase, renovation and resale of specific homes. Instead, he splurged the money on personal expenses, unrelated business costs and payments to earlier investors.

Says US Attorney Ryan Raybould,

“Financial fraud isn’t just numbers on a ledger—it’s a direct assault on hardworking Americans who trusted an alleged expert with their savings. Carrier didn’t just target investors; he preyed on Main Street families, retirees and small business owners through a sham ‘We Buy Ugly Houses’ scam. Through his lies and deceit, Carrier earned every month of his 15-year sentence. This case should serve as a warning to those who target Main Street Americans in North Texas.”

FBI Dallas Special Agent in Charge R. Joseph Rothrcok notes that the sentence highlights the damage caused by investment fraud and urged the public to research opportunities carefully.
